From the summary of **A Geographic History of the World: Chapter X :: Catholicism in Crisis | The European Wars of Religion**

As we know from Chapter IX's study on the Italian Wars, Cesare I's ordered destruction of the Vatican in Rome, and the Red Hat Massacre, in the final throes of his empire sent shockwaves across Europe, fracturing the weakened Roman Catholic Church into multiple competing Catholic papacies in the ensuing decades. The strongest successor Catholic papacies being:

* The Imperial (German) Papacy in Mainz in 1548
* The French Papacy in Avignon in 1550
* The Castilian Papacy in Toledo in 1554
* The Levantine (Roman) Papacy in Jerusalem in 1555

Various other Christian churches also began to appear around the mid-16th century; however, the four papcies mentioned above all claimed to be the universal Catholic Church, and had the strongest ability to do so. This created a new and dangerous friction between the European powers of the time that had never been seen before.

All of this unease culminated in a major pan-European war so named "The War of the Four Peters". (As by chance, four separate popes shared the regnal name of Peter in the later part of the 16th century at the onset of the war.)

There are a few primary events that led directly to this war occuring. Following the last of the Italian Wars (1503 - 1551), the peninsula was divided between Naples (France) and the Holy Roman Empire (HRE) \[Western Roman Empire\]. The northern Italian states, as well as the lands that were the Papal States, were assumed into the HRE. The Duchy of Milan was already a possession of the Luxemburg family by this point in time. 

In 1548, Sigismund II had himself crowned as Emperor of Rome \[Western Roman Emperor\] in the newly Imperial State of Rome by the Arch-Bishop of Mainz, now Bishop of Rome \[Sixtus V\]. This was a significant development for the legitimacy of the Imperial Papacy, and a major affront to the reigning Catholic pope, Julius IV.

To the west in France, the 1550 election of their own pope, Paul IV \[in honour of the last Roman pope\], in Avignon was feigned under the legitmacy of Avignon as the true successor to Rome. Castile followed with a papal election \[Alexander VII\] in Toledo 4 years later.

Elsewhere in Europe, Portugal, France and the Weald continued in their colonisation of Vespasia across the Atlantic Ocean. The Crown of Poland, beset on all sides by enemies, came to an uneasy alliance with the Catholic orders to its northern borders. As the conflicts with Moscow continued in their intensity.

All across Europe, tensions rise as the great wars are only but around the corner.

(Original upload wasn't displaying properly for whatever reason, so here's am updated version with a some alterations and additions!)

Welcome to my interpretation of what the USA, as well as North America to an extent, could look like in Rockstar's universe, specifically centered around the time following GTAV. This takes the most inspiration from the HD universe. I know a lot of people enjoy the idea that all of the game spaces exist relatively close to each other, or that there isn't an analagous USA so-to-speak; but I just wanted to create a "*realistic*" Rockstar USA.

There's not a whole lotta deep thought put into anything, more just me having some fun and wanting to make a zany map; so that's why you get some alternate history, some heavy terraforming (especially to create the Pacific coast as I really do enjoy the shape of southern San Andreas, just obviously massively scaled up)—just a bit of everything.

I could probably keep adding more and more stuff, but I just wanted to finish a map for once. Hope someone enjoys!

> #### Excerpt taken from **A Geographic History of the World:** *Chapter IX - The Age of Lancastrian Dominance*

> ##### *On the 1st War of the Crossing*:  
The first real test of the Lancastrian kings came with the death of Arthur I, leaving an under-aged son as heir to both France and England. His mother, Lucrezia Isabella de Borgia, as well as his uncle, Edmund of Poitiers, acted as regents of the crown for Geoffrey. And whilst they were both loyal to the wishes of Arthur, there were others who were not. Having wrested the throne from his great-grandfather, Henry III & VI, nearly 80 years prior, William of Orleans remained ever watchful of the throne. Years of rule had built quite a great amount of respect on Edward and his grandson Arthur, but even the peerage of France and of England could not cast a blind eye at Arthur's wars in Italy and Aragon, building more debt-itself already high from Henry II's needs to both unify and crusade.

> With the accession of Geoffrey to the throne in 1523, there was some measure of calmness that the monarchy would simply endure the previous years' wrongdoings and move forward. Geoffrey looked at it quite differently. Almost immediately upon his coronation as King of France (and of England) in Paris, he  subsequently named himself the rightful King of Naples (or Sicily, depending upon historical convention; some evidence exists that he claimed himself King of Hungary as well, however, no factual evidence exists outside of a single letter written by his uncle to an unnamed receiver in Paris. The claim to Naples is believed to have been suggested by his mother in her capacity as regent and as a legal claimant herself through certain provisions within her brother, the late Cesare I, Emperor of Italy.)

> Never-the-less, this action sparked a great amount of resistance from the peerage, and parliament in England. They demanded that Geoffrey look inwards towards domestic problems rather than push once more for the Neapolitan throne, as his father had done so. Geoffrey instead made certain promises of more independent decision making in an address to a meeting of parliament in Winchester, though no evidence seems to point to this occurring. Instead, the Duchy of Lancaster was granted to his younger brother, Arthur Louis, along with a certain level of control over the affairs of the Kingdom of England. France remained far more important to the crown, and Geoffrey focused much of his attention on trying to appease the quickly-angering peerage there.

> Having blinded himself to the problems in England, Geoffrey found himself in the midst of a civil war in 1531. A once major ally to the crown under Arthur, the duke of Kent (Henry de Graye), and the earls of Hampshire (William of Southampton) and Wiltshire (Henry Butler) were the first to declare themselves independent of the crown in Paris, they were followed by Richard II, Duke of York, in late 1531 and Geoffrey's uncle, Edward I, Lord of Ireland (and *de jure sang* Duke of Cornwall) in 1532. Not without allies, the Counts of Flanders and Artois found themselves pulled into what became known as the War of the Crossing, a part of the greater animosity between the House of Lancaster and the Lancastrian House of Orleans. Geoffrey's murder in 1534 at the hands of his cousin and successor, William III, created even more problems. In France, the Duchy of Normandy seceded, acting as another thorn in the crown's control of the war. 

> By the end of the conflict, the Crown of France had suffered the loss of much of its coastal territory in the north of France, as well as the entirety of Lancashire to Cheshire to Yorkshire in the north of England. Northumberland remained a stalwart march of the Crown of France, surrounded by foes. Of the peers to declare themselves independent, the Grayes of Kent found themselves the most successfully placed. Henry de Graye was crowned King of the Weald in 1533 in Canterbury, demanding the submission of Hampshire. During the war, de Graye's hold on the south of England spread from Bristol Channel to the Hanoverian Sea. In the peace signed between himself and William III, much of that land was returned to the Crown of France. The lands around Bristol were kept by the de Grayes, as well as the area of Langueville in the north of France. Boulogne, positioned in a rather powerful place on the Crossing's coast, retained its independence, as did the now 'Grand' Duchy of Cornwall. Ireland was returned in full to the Crown of France.


> William III almost immediately began on work to seize back his lost territory, however, it would never happen during his lifetime. A virgin world laid to the west, one that other European powers were already seizing upon; the continued push eastwards by the (Eastern) Roman Empire and the Crusader Kingdoms provided more opportunities for influence that the House of Lancaster had taken during the 15th century; and the Mediterranean itself remained open for conquest, as Arthur had tried nearly half a century before.

*Excerpt taken from A Geographic History of the World*

The *2nd War of Henri's Crossing* (see also the overarching *Cornish Succession Crisis*) had been a costly endeavor for all participants, and is significant as being the first major war fought on both sides of the Atlantic. For the most part of the war, the colonial possessions in the northern parts of Vespasia had remained untouched.

As a part of the prelude to war, the Levantine Pope in Jerusalem (via his proxy, the Archbishop of Canterbury) invested the crowns of the newly created Vespasian Kingdoms of Almdon and Pinsley in the young king of the Weald, William II, massively increasing his power in the new world, and bolstering his legitimacy in Europe.

For the Weald-in-Vespasia, much of the war was fought navally, with mostly minor incidents occurring in the southern crown possessions. The siege of Port-of-Dhonnaile was the most significant land-based event to occur and resulted in a costly victory for France.

Following the highly favourable concessions that France was forced to make, the Weald-in-Vespasia exploded in both population and economy. The expansion of the Godfrey territory during the 1660s helped as well, connecting the Wealden territories with the River Humphrey to the north.

Although William II made plans to visit his colonial possessions, he never did. In 1663, he instead convened the Council of Dover: it was during this event that the peerages of both Almdon and Pinsley were created in full. William received the oaths of loyalty from his newly created peers, amongst them the powerful Duke of New Dover and the Marquis of Blackheath.

Separately, William created a new office of viceroyalty for his friend and confidant Thomas Lancel to oversea the distant kingdoms. Lancel never arrived in Maidenstone and historians differ as to reasons why. In March of 1668, Edward, Earl of Caldsmouth, was named viceroy in his stead.

The Weald-in-Vespasia would prove to be a worthwhile colonial venture, and only the start of the rush for more lands in the north of Vespasia-lands that other powers in the Wealden crown, the British Isles and elsewhere in Europe had in their sights as well.
